newsitem.title: UK: High blood pressure patients minus molecule -study.
newsitem.headline: High blood pressure patients minus molecule -study.

text.p: A team of British doctors said on Friday they had identified a possible new target for treating high blood pressure -- a common body chemical known as nitric oxide.
Nitric oxide, or NO, is involved not only regulating blood pressure regulation but also in a wide variety of physical responses from brain function to erection.
Nigel Benjamin, a clinical pharmacologist at London's St Batholomew's Hospital, and colleagues conducted a two-part study to see how much NO was produced by people with high blood pressure.
Reporting in the Lancet medical journal, they said they first put 10 patients with high blood pressure and 13 healthy controls on a low-nitrate diet for two days.
They found that high blood pressure patients lost less nitrate in their urine than the control group.
In a second test, 11 blood pressure patients and 11 healthy controls were put on a limited nitrate diet and then injected with radioactively labelled arginine, which the body turns into NO.
The doctors found that the higher a person's blood pressure, the less nitrate was excreted.
"The results of this study provide evidence that NO production is lower in patients with essential hypertension than in healthy people," they wrote.
But they said it was not clear whether high blood pressure affected NO or whether an imbalance of NO caused high blood pressure.
"It would be interesting to find out whether our results are affected by treatment with antihypertensive drugs," they said.
Standard treatments for high blood pressure include calcium-channel blockers, which prevent calcium from accumulating in the muscle cells of the heart and blood vessels.
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors block formation of angiotensin II, which can close capillaries and force the heart to work harder.
